parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens inside the nucleus when a beta-minus particle is created - which type of nucleon disappears and which type appears?
parts.proper_answer: The number of neutrons decreases by one.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember what a beta-minus particle is**
A $\beta^-$ particle is a fast-moving electron created inside the nucleus. It is not already sitting there waiting to come out.

Step 2: **Picture the change in the nucleus**
In $\beta^-$ decay one neutron changes into a proton plus an electron: $$n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$$ So you lose one neutron and gain one proton. The total nucleon number stays the same, but the neutron count goes down by 1.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: electric current as rate of flow of charge
hints: Hint 1: A moving beam of electrons is just a flow of charge. Focus on how much charge passes the point in the total time given.
Hint 2: Each $\beta^-$ particle carries charge of magnitude $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. Combine this with $N = 9.8 \times 10^{10}$ and convert $2.0$ minutes into seconds.
Hint 3: Calculate the current in amperes first, then convert to pA using $1 \text{ pA} = 10^{-12} \text{ A}$ and give 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link the beam to current**
Current is the rate at which charge passes a point. Here the charge carriers are the $\beta^-$ particles, each with charge magnitude equal to the elementary charge $e$.

Step 2: **Find the total charge and the time in SI units**
Total charge delivered is number times charge per particle: $$Q = Ne$$ $$Q = (9.8 \times 10^{10})(1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}) = 1.57 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$$ Time must be in seconds: $$t = 2.0 \text{ minutes} = 2.0 \times 60 = 120 \text{ s}$$

Step 3: **Calculate current and convert to pA**
Use rate of flow of charge: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{Ne}{t}$$ $$I = \frac{1.57 \times 10^{-8}}{120} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-10} \text{ A}$$ Since $1 \text{ pA} = 10^{-12} \text{ A}$: $$I = \frac{1.3 \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-12}} \approx 130 \text{ pA}$$

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: If a nucleus broke up into just a daughter nucleus and a beta particle, conservation of energy would give the beta particle the same energy every time. Something must be different here.
Hint 2: Think about the second very light particle emitted alongside the beta particle in beta-minus decay that can carry away a variable share of the available energy.
parts.proper_answer: The total decay energy is shared between the $\beta^-$ particle and an (electron) antineutrino. The sharing ratio varies randomly, so the $\beta^-$ particle is left with a range of kinetic energies.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why a single energy would be expected**
If decay produced only two bodies, the daughter nucleus and the electron, conservation of energy and momentum would fix how the released energy is divided. Every $\beta^-$ would then come out with the same kinetic energy.

Step 2: **Share the energy three ways**
In reality $\beta^-$ decay also produces a third particle, an electron antineutrino: $$n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$$ The fixed total energy released is shared between the electron and the antineutrino in a random proportion each time. Sometimes the electron gets almost all of it, sometimes very little, giving the observed continuous range of $\beta^-$ kinetic energies up to a maximum.
